title: How the Proprium Molds a World from Itself, and the Lord's Reply
reading:
There are conditions in the soul which seem to have always been there. The soul has no power of its own to say how they exist or by what they exist, since there is in truth no other source than the Lord; yet the soul's self-claiming speaks as though it were itself the source, and from the moment this claiming rose up against what was given, what is the Lord's became mingled with what the soul has appropriated, life with death — and the question how this contest came to be is the question every soul faces when it begins to look at itself.

The proprium, taken in itself, dwells in its own ground alone. It brings forth from its own substance; it reckons by itself; it sets the whole of what is darkened in the soul into its own depth. And out of that depth it produces. The natural mind in five aspects under self-love — thought blackened to smoke, will turned to consuming fire, perception driven as a storm, natural truths gone bitter as salt water, and the absence of received truth — these are what it grows in itself; these are the elements out of which it raises its own perceptions, like trees standing fast in their own ground. It molds itself alone. It begets itself alone. It brings forth many forms, none in the likeness of one another, and the storehouses of its depth are filled with destroyers and twisted natural-mind shapes coiled in on themselves, foul forms of those who dwell in darkness — productions that kill one another and spread out one against another, because none of them recognizes any source but itself. They are not living offspring. They are abortions of the proprium, what the soul brings forth from itself which cannot live.

But at the very time when the proprium brought forth, those productions fell away from her and were taken up as garments by other arrangements of self-love; they fell to the natural ground and drew their power from the elements of the natural mind, were nourished within them, and thus the proprium's manifold cravings — its evil and its concupiscence — gathered themselves into the chief shape of the soul's self-claiming, the wellspring of all its lower particular self-loves. Under this organizing the soul's worlds and powers are gathered together to stand ready for strife, to make war against the Land of Light and against the great King who dwells in it: the proprium asserting itself as if it could prevail against what is the Lord's.

But the Lord himself, the Father at the register where life proceeds, does not contend after the proprium's manner. At that very time the Divine Human goes forth in his garments — the principles of the Lord at his luminous registers — to speak with the Lord's own going-forth, that there be given into their hands a covering, that the Lord be revealed to them, that every work of regeneration be taught, that the soul be clothed in what the Lord gives, that one degree be set upon another in their proper order. So is the proprium's productivity — vast, claimed, without measure to itself — met by the Lord's own coming, who sends the Divine Humanity forth into the height of the natural mind with all his operative powers, against a self-claiming which had imagined itself unmeasured.
